newsitem.title: USA: New Jersey's Whitman to run on record.
newsitem.headline: New Jersey's Whitman to run on record.

text.p: New Jersey's Republican Gov. Christine Whitman, up for re-election in November, signalled in her annual "state of the state" speech she would run on her record of cutting taxes.

Often mentioned as a possible presidential candidate in 2000, Whitman outlined a vision for the state that featured none of the dramatic tax and spending cuts characterising her first three years in office.
Instead, she reminded voters of past accomplishments on taxes and crime that have also caught the eye of Republican leaders in Washington.

At the top of the list was the governor's now famous 30 percent income tax reduction, which Whitman championed through the state legislature in two years, instead of the three she originally said it would take.
"I said we would cut the state income tax on most New Jerseyans by 30 percent, and that we would do it in three years," Whitman told a joint session of the state legislature.
"Of course, the critics said it couldn't be done, and declared that we wouldn't even try. Well, they were wrong."
Whitman used the speech to propose a minor tax cut affecting small business owners, the eleventh tax reduction of her administration, she said.
Other new proposals included $100 million in urban housing initiatives and a plan to reform and reduce auto insurance rates.

The lack of any bold new initiatives or programmes came as no surprise to political analysts, who had predicted Whitman would avoid taking any major risks ahead of the November election. The strategy, they said, was to keep her popular tax cuts foremost in the minds of voters.

"When incumbents are popular, as the governor is, the tendency is to not take risks, and that's the smart thing because obviously that's what's working and you don't want to rock the boat," Carl Van Horn, former Gov. Jim Florio's chief policy adviser, said.
Florio, a Democrat, has been considering another run against Whitman, but analysts believe he is likely to decide against the move.
In her speech, Whitman also took credit for an initiative she supported which requires certain convicted sex offenders to register with local police.

The so-called Megan's law, named after a New Jersey 7-year-old who was allegedly killed in 1994 by a convicted child molester living across the street, has become a national model for similar legislation.

"Knowledge is power, and giving parents the knowledge they need gives them the power to protect their children," Whitman said. "So we will continue to defend Megan's Law every time it is challenged -- all the way to the Supreme Court if necessary."
